summary: A 1977 note on writing network addresses as a set of fields that can be extended by adding fields on the left or right, or by making fields bigger. It was motivated by a larger address space in the host and IMP interface.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 730 proposes writing network addresses as named parts rather than one combined number. New parts could identify a network or a component inside a host, and existing fields could grow.

questions: why do network addresses need fields
how can addresses grow over time
subtitle: A proposal to represent network addresses as named fields that can grow independently.

tldr.problem: Changes to host and IMP address sizes can break software that treats their fields as one number, while internetworking and multiprocessor hosts need more address structure.
tldr.mechanism: The memo proposes named decimal fields, separated by slashes, that can be extended by adding fields or increasing a field's size.
tldr.outcome: The proposal describes how field-based addresses could accommodate network scope and finer structure within a host.

today: RFC 730 is a proposal for extensible field-based addressing. The memo asks that addresses be represented by fields so their scope and detail can grow.

sections.title: Why Address Fields Need Room to Grow
sections.content:
The revised Host-IMP interface increased the sizes of its host and IMP fields. Software that treated the earlier fields as a single number could therefore have difficulty with the new addresses.

The memo also considers connecting multiple networks and addressing multiple processors or emulated hosts behind one network connection.
sections.plainLanguage: Address fields can change size as a network grows. Addresses may also need extra parts to identify connected networks or parts inside a host.

sections.title: Named Fields
sections.content:
The proposal writes an address as a field name, a colon, and decimal fields separated by slashes. The suggested hierarchy is Network, IMP, Host, and Message-Identifier, from the most general field to more specific ones.

For example, the RFC uses NET:1/3/5/7 to identify message identifier 7 at host 5 on IMP 3 in network 1. It uses HOST:6 for host 6 on the local IMP.
sections.plainLanguage: The address states what its first field means, then gives increasingly specific values. The slash-separated fields make the hierarchy visible.

sections.title: Extending the Address
sections.content:
The RFC describes three ways to extend a field-based address: make an individual field larger, add fields on the left to increase scope for internetworks, or add fields on the right to describe finer structure within a host.

It points to places where people enter addresses, including TIP open and Telnet or FTP connect commands, as areas where the notation would be visible.
sections.plainLanguage: Fields can grow independently. Adding them on the left can name a broader network, and adding them on the right can identify a smaller part of a host.
